subject: Computer Networking
title: Ransomware
description: A fast breakdown of Ransomware for builders.

hook.text: You open a file. Minutes later, every document is encrypted. A message demands $500,000 in Bitcoin.

buildup.text: Ransomware encrypts your files with a key only the attacker holds. Pay the ransom, maybe get the key. Maybe not.

discovery.text: It spreads through phishing, unpatched systems, and exposed remote desktop. Once inside, it moves fast.

twist.text: Paying the ransom funds more attacks. But some organizations pay because they have no backups and can't operate.

climax.text: The Colonial Pipeline attack in 2021 shut down fuel supply to the U.S. East Coast. Ransom paid: $4.4 million.

punchline.text: Backups are the best defense. If you can restore, the ransom doesn't matter.

quiz.question: What is the best defense against ransomware?
options: Regular, tested backups stored separately from the network

details.summary: Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key. Modern ransomware also exfiltrates data before encryption, threatening to publish it if the ransom is not paid. It is the most financially damaging form of cybercrime, costing billions annually.
details.whyItMatters: Ransomware can halt an entire organization's operations in minutes. Prevention through backups, patching, and segmentation is critical because recovery without paying is often impossible.
takeaways: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment for decryption
Double extortion adds data theft and publication threats
Offline backups are the most reliable defense against ransomware

faq.question: Should you pay ransomware demands?
faq.answer: Law enforcement generally advises against paying because it funds criminal operations and does not guarantee data recovery. However, organizations without viable backups sometimes pay when the alternative is permanent data loss or business closure. Prevention is far better than facing this choice.

faq.question: How do you protect against ransomware?
faq.answer: Maintain offline backups that ransomware cannot reach. Keep all systems patched to close exploitation paths. Segment networks to limit spread. Train users to recognize phishing. Use endpoint detection and response tools. Test backup restoration regularly to ensure recovery actually works.
